questions.q: Newton's cannonball thought experiment shows that an orbit is best understood as:
options: An object held up against gravity by a balancing outward force
An object continuously falling toward the Earth while moving sideways so fast that the curved Earth keeps falling away beneath it
An object in a region where gravity has switched off
An object pushed outward by centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Fired fast enough horizontally, the cannonball falls toward the Earth but the round surface curves away by the same amount, so it never lands — it falls around the Earth. An orbiting satellite is in continuous free fall.

questions.q: Why are astronauts on the ISS (~400 km up) weightless, even though gravity there is still close to 90% of its surface value?
options: Because gravity is nearly zero at that altitude
Because they and their spacecraft are all in free fall together, with no supporting force pushing up from below
Because the Earth's magnetic field cancels gravity
Because the station spins to balance gravity with centrifugal force
questions.explanation: Weightlessness is not the absence of gravity — at ISS altitude the field strength is still close to 9 N/kg. The astronauts feel weightless because they are falling around the Earth with their craft, experiencing only gravity with no normal force underneath them.

questions.q: Setting gravitational force equal to centripetal force, what happens to the mass of the satellite, and what does the orbital speed depend on?
options: The satellite mass doubles the speed; speed depends on satellite mass and radius
The satellite mass cancels; orbital speed depends only on the central mass and the orbital radius, giving \(v = \sqrt{GM/r}\)
The satellite mass must be added to Earth's mass; speed depends on their sum
The satellite mass sets a minimum altitude for orbit
questions.explanation: Equating \(GMm/r^2 = mv^2/r\), the satellite mass appears on both sides and cancels, leaving \(v = \sqrt{GM/r}\). A bolt and a space station at the same altitude orbit at the same speed — the same reason Galileo's heavy and light balls fall together.

questions.q: Within Low Earth Orbit, what bounds the usable band from below and from above?
options: The ozone layer below and the Moon's gravity above
Atmospheric drag below about 200-250 km, and the Van Allen radiation belts above about 1000 km
Escape velocity below and the geostationary altitude above
Air pressure below and the solar wind above
questions.explanation: Below ~200-250 km, residual atmosphere causes drag that decays the orbit (Mir came down largely this way). Above ~1000 km lie the Van Allen belts of trapped charged particles that can damage electronics and endanger astronauts. LEO is the clear band between them.

questions.q: What distinguishes a geostationary orbit from a merely geosynchronous one?
options: A geostationary orbit is much lower and faster than a geosynchronous one

Both have a one-day period, but a geostationary orbit must lie over the equator with zero tilt and a circular path so it appears motionless, while a tilted geosynchronous orbit traces a daily figure-eight
A geosynchronous orbit appears motionless but a geostationary one drifts
Geostationary refers to GPS satellites, geosynchronous to weather satellites
questions.explanation: Both share a one-day period. A geostationary orbit is the special case with zero inclination (equatorial) and a circular path, so it hangs still. A tilted geosynchronous orbit (like Syncom 2) traces a daily figure-eight. All geostationary orbits are geosynchronous, but not vice versa.

questions.q: GPS positioning works by trilateration. Why are a minimum of FOUR satellites needed for a fix, not three?
options: To average out random signal noise

Three could fix the three spatial coordinates, but the receiver's cheap clock has an unknown error that corrupts all the distances; the fourth satellite supplies the extra equation to solve for that clock error too
Because one satellite is always a backup in case another fails
To measure the angles between the satellites
questions.explanation: Each satellite distance (travel time × speed of light) gives one equation. Three could pin the three coordinates, but the receiver's clock error is a fourth unknown corrupting every distance. A fourth satellite gives the fourth equation, solving for position and clock error simultaneously — and correcting the cheap clock for free.

questions.q: Why were GPS atomic clocks deliberately built to tick at the 'wrong' frequency before launch?
options: To save battery power in orbit
Because the net of two relativistic effects makes an orbiting clock run fast by about 38 microseconds per day, so building it to run slow on the ground makes it tick correctly once in orbit
Because the cold of space speeds clocks up unpredictably
Because a slower signal is easier for receivers to lock onto
questions.explanation: Special relativity (motion) loses ~7.2 µs/day; general relativity (weaker gravity at altitude) gains ~45.9 µs/day; the net is ~38 µs/day fast. Engineers set the clocks to ~10.22999999543 MHz instead of 10.23 MHz so that, once relativity speeds them up, they tick at the right rate.

questions.q: From memory: explain Newton's cannonball thought experiment and how it shows that an orbiting satellite is in free fall.
keyPoints: A cannon on an impossibly tall mountain fires a ball horizontally; faster shots travel further before landing.
Because the Earth is round, if the ball is fast enough the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, so it never lands — it falls around the Earth forever.
An orbiting satellite is therefore in continuous free fall: gravity still acts fully, but the satellite moves sideways fast enough to perpetually miss the planet.
Above escape velocity (~11.2 km/s for Earth) the object breaks free and never returns instead of orbiting.
questions.explanation: If you captured the 'always falling but always missing the Earth' idea and linked it to free fall, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: name the two relativistic effects on a GPS satellite clock, which theory each comes from, and which way each pushes.
keyPoints: Special relativity (motion): a fast-moving clock runs slow — the satellite at ~3.9 km/s loses about 7.2 µs/day.
General relativity (gravity): a clock higher up in weaker gravity runs fast — the satellite gains about 45.9 µs/day.
The two do not cancel; the gravitational gain is larger, so the net is the clock running fast by about 38 µs/day.
Ignoring this would drift every fix by ~11.5 km on the first day, making GPS useless.
questions.explanation: If you correctly assigned 'slow from motion' to special relativity and 'fast from weaker gravity' to general relativity, and knew the gravitational effect dominates, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: The geostationary orbital radius is about 42 164 km measured from Earth's centre. Earth's radius is about 6 378 km. Find the altitude of a geostationary satellite above the ground.
questions.explanation: Kepler's law gives the radius from Earth's centre; you must subtract Earth's radius to get the altitude above the surface. The result, ~35 786 km, is the figure Arthur Clarke worked out by hand in 1945.

questions.q: A GPS satellite clock runs fast by a net 38 microseconds per day. Convert that timing error to a distance using the speed of light to find how far off a position fix would drift on the first day if relativity were ignored.
questions.given: timing error \(\Delta t = 38\,\mu\mathrm{s} = 38\times10^{-6}\,\mathrm{s}\),  speed of light \(c = 3.0\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
questions.explanation: Because GPS multiplies time by the speed of light, even 38 millionths of a second becomes about 11.5 km of error in a single day — growing daily until navigation places you in the wrong city. This is why the relativistic correction is not optional.
